questions.tip: Keep it to about a minute: school, activities, skills, and why this job. Stick to school and accomplishments, not social life.
questions.from: Illinois workNet: Top 10 questions with minimal experience

questions.q: Why do you want this job?
questions.tip: Say how your school, club or volunteer skills fit this job. Name one real thing about the place.
questions.from: Illinois workNet: Top 10 questions with minimal experience

questions.q: What do you know about us?
questions.tip: Look at their website or visit first. Say one specific thing you noticed. Do not recite facts.
questions.from: Illinois workNet: Top 10 questions with minimal experience

questions.tip: Use your school, volunteering and other experience as proof. Pick two things.
questions.from: Illinois workNet: Top 10 questions with minimal experience

questions.q: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
questions.tip: Name strengths adults have praised. For a weakness, be honest, pick one that does not rule you out for this job, and say what you are doing about it.
questions.from: Cal Poly Pomona career center: 9 interview tips for teens

questions.q: What days and hours can you work?
questions.tip: Bring a proposed weekly schedule. Give the hours per week and the days you cannot work. Do not say "whenever." Use the availability planner above.
questions.from: Cal Poly Pomona career center: 9 interview tips for teens

questions.q: Tell me about a time you worked on a team.
questions.tip: Have three or four short stories ready from school, clubs, sports or family jobs. Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
questions.from: Cal Poly Pomona career center: 9 interview tips for teens

questions.q: Tell me about a time you made a mistake or handled something difficult.
questions.tip: Same stories, same STAR steps. Say what you learned and what you do differently now.
questions.from: NYC Summer Youth Employment Program training guide

questions.q: What do you hope to learn from this job?
questions.tip: Match skills you already have to what the job needs, then say what you want to get better at.
questions.from: Illinois workNet: Top 10 questions with minimal experience

questions.q: Where do you see yourself in a few years?
questions.tip: Keep it short and clear: how you want to grow and gain experience.
questions.from: Illinois workNet: Top 10 questions with minimal experience

questions.q: What does a day at this job look like to you?
questions.tip: Be general, and mention managing your time to finish tasks.

questions.tip: Always have two. See the list below.

ask: What does a normal workday look like?
What are the biggest challenges in this job?
What would success look like in this job?
What is the next step, and when will I hear back?

askSource.t: Addison Public Library: job tips for teens

day: Arrive about 10 minutes early. The sources say 5 to 15, and the reason is paperwork.
Bring extra copies of your resume, a pen and a small pad.
Phone off or on silent. Firm handshake and eye contact.
Dress to match what staff wear there. For a casual first job, neat pants and a collared shirt or polo is a safe pick.
A parent can help you practice and give you a ride, but should not come in with you.
pay: Sources disagree on asking about pay in a first interview. Illinois workNet says wait until you get an offer. A public library guide and a university career center say it is okay to ask, as long as it is not your only question. The posting often states the pay already, so check there first.

thanks.timing: Send a thank-you note or email within 1 to 2 days. One note, and at most one polite check-in after that.
lines: Say you are still interested in the job.
Say one way you can help.

source.t: Illinois workNet: tips for youth applying

rules: Have four people ready, and list as many as the form asks.
Good choices: a teacher, a coach, a family you babysit for, a boss or volunteer supervisor.
Ask each person first. Do not write someone down without telling them.
Give their name plus a phone number or email.

source.t: Minnesota CareerForce: 10 job search tips for teens

refs.gap: The sources do not say whether a parent, relative or youth pastor can be a reference. If a form says no relatives, use a teacher, coach or supervisor.

app: Decide your days and hours before you start.
Fill every box. Write N/A if a section does not apply.
With no job history, list babysitting, yard work, club roles and volunteering. Volunteering counts as job history.
Do not write that you will take "any" job. Be flexible on hours and specific about the job.
Keep one document with your address, phone, school, and volunteer or work dates and phone numbers.
Be ready for an interview on the spot when you drop off an application.
evidence: Practice helps you feel prepared. We looked for a study showing that interview practice gets typical teens hired and did not find one. The best data are about students with disabilities, and they show a link, not proof of cause.

evidenceSource.t: PubMed Central: virtual interview practice and jobs

gaps: Whether a parent, relative or youth pastor can be a reference.
What to do if you have no babysitting or volunteer history either.
Phone, video and group interviews (the career site that covers them was blocked).
Modest, religious or uniform dress at an interview.
Which questions an employer cannot ask you. Ask your state labor agency.
